blocks.x: Let's get your name and see if it's going...
Yeah, well, let's see, where's the microphone on there?
It's right here.
Right on the top there, right?
So you don't even have to... It picked us up. Uh-huh. Melvin.
1973, and we were talking about the post office and how the special delivery jobs were going to whites only.

That's right. And I had passed examination, so I got the job, and they assumed that they thought I was white. And I was driving a brand new Buick and some of these other old carcassers, and they had these old Model As and cars like that. The first real bad incident came up when I, after I was in there a while, I went upstairs and used the restroom. And the next day when I came in, the supervisor, I remember his name real well, was Ducco. He called me and says, hey Dominic, he said, did you use that restroom upstairs? Yes, I certainly did. He said, well don't you know that's not your restroom. Your restroom is around the corner, which was about a half a block down the street. I said, what do you mean? So he was trying to tell me that that restroom upstairs was for white only, and I had to go to the next one, which was designated as to. So I just, with the, I'm very hot-headed, and I just told him, I said, I may never use that restroom again. I said, but I want to let you know this, that if I feel like I need a restroom and I'm here, then you're going to have to get ready to tell me again about it, because I'm going to use it. Well, that didn't set so well with him, and then now they finally realize that I'm a Negro, and all these other white characters in there. And so they finally decided to open up another slot, there was a Negro boy there, his name was Conley, very nice looking fellow, he'd just come back from the Korean War, I think it was, I don't know exactly which one it was, but he had come back and they had given him a job. So this day I walked in there and I was sorting out my mail, and my car was parked in that little alley up there on Union Street, and this fellow coming in and renting and panning, and who was that old raggedy automobile for out there? So I told Mr. Duke Cross, and Mr. Duke Roller, after I sorted out my mail, he's talking about my car, I said it's not blocking anything, do you want me to remove it? So he said, yeah, it's going to remove it, and shut his mouth up. So when I turned around, I grabbed him in the neck, and it's going to hit him. So this guy says, cool it down, and he says, I'm starting up in the middle, so I caught myself. I knew I needed to work, I'd gone broke, see. And all of this is piling up within me also. So I went on the outside, and got to my car, and I used to carry a little piece of iron pipe in the inch behind, because the drivers around there were so irritated, man, I figured one day something might happen, and I'd have to defend myself. So he walked on the outside, man, there's a little cement porch, and I went and I talked to him, I said, look, let me tell you one thing, I said, I didn't come here begging for this job, I said, I passed an examination for this job. That's how he got it, and I said, boy, I know you can't even read and write your name, which he couldn't. But he had gotten a job in the days when you just could come into the post office and get a job. So he told me, I got to remember, well, what he was trying to tell me, I have to remember, this is the words of some of the old die hard crackers, as you call them. He was trying to tell me that I got to remember, he was a white man, and I was a nigger. So he never did get the words out, I didn't get my piece of iron, and I put it on his head, and I told him to finish what he started to say. Well, in the meantime, all these other carriers came out to see what was happening, heard the promotion, I told him, it's not me you're worried about, it's him, because I'd say if you finish this, tell me what he started to tell me, I said, you're going to have to pick him up. So they brought him inside, and Conley was standing on the outside, he told me about Conley, he called me after, it was a nickname that's going on. through the ages with me, he said, I was going to help him out, and we put out a switch plate, so I told him no, I said, don't do that Conley, I said, you're going to live here, I said, I'm not going to live here, I said, I can't live in this city. So I came home and I told Hazel to start packing, and we're going back to San Antonio, job or no job. So we packed up and we came back, and then I started working on Hayden, Fats Markins Band, which was the remnants of my band. But he was still a real contretto fellow, and he had his own ways, and he was, well I imagine, maybe I can put it this way, that the bar wasn't well, nobody knew, and he finally was getting to the place where he was getting sick all the time. And maybe that's why he was irritable all the time with me. So I stayed with him a while, and we played around him until I went to work in the civil service. And incidentally, Herbert Hall worked around me with us too.
In the civil service?
Yeah, I got him a job, I got a fancy job. All the music wasn't doing so good. So I told him, I said, well let's go to work, let's give us a job.
I'm having a hard time straightening that all out now. Civil service first, then you quit in 40, late 40, then 43 you quit, then 40 opened up the keyhole. Now when did you go back to New Orleans?

No, when I went to New Orleans in 45, 48. 48. And I stayed there for one year, in the post office. And then I came back to San Antonio in 50, to open this other keyhole, this new keyhole, that's on Poplar Street.
You were only a year in the post office? That's all I knew. Because you know, I had, Orrin Blackstone had met you, I don't know if you remember him.
Orrin Blackstone was the first one that wrote that article on me. I still have that little book, whether it was Playback or something like that. He was up on Verone Street. Yeah, 439.
That's right. So that's when I just missed you, see I had just come to New Orleans.
Yeah.
And I heard about you through Orrin, because Orrin thought something like that. Right.
But I met him, he came to the house down there. That was the first story that actually came out on me. That was the first.
Well, he's very few people know about Orrin today.
Right.
He's forgotten.
But whatever happened to him?
He met Mr. Slidell, and he's a newspaper man, and he's retired.

You know, I sure would like to write him a letter. If you get by chance, can talk to him or send me his address. I have it with me. Well, good, we'll get it before you leave. I know he'd be surprised. I haven't talked to him since he wrote the story.
Yeah. Well, of course, he and I went in the record business together. Oh, you did?

Yeah. And I worked with him. Well, this other Keyhole Nightclub was a fantastic place. It was the first integrated club in the entire South, which you can consider fully integrated. Now, when was this?
1950. 1950. 1950. Easter Saturday. Easter Saturday. Saturday before Easter. Right. Which they called Easter Saturday. Yeah.
And you opened it up and it was first for the integrated.
That's right. Did you have any kind of trouble with the law?

No trouble until after we had operated around and I had gotten all of the business in town, the other clubs were suffering. And the white operators got together themselves. They did everything they could to get the policemen to close the place. And, of course, the liquor control laws in those days had gotten to the place where at 12 o'clock at night you'd have to stop operating and stop drinking. But I was able to operate in our club until 2, 3 o'clock in the morning, not serving any drinks and not having any intoxicated beverages on the premises. People had mostly to see the shows. So, finally when the administration changed and we got some real die-hards in there and they didn't agree with the policy of the keyhole and they closed it down. Supposedly they put padlocks on the board. So, we went to Colt with him and I got an injunction against the police department. They couldn't even come on the premises or not even pass in front of the, close to the premises a certain amount of feet. And, when I went to Colt with him it cost about $18,000 plus the business to win the case. When I won the case for the keyhole, I not only integrated the keyhole, I integrated the state of Texas. Judge Sanders, he's dead, passed a decision. He told him, he says, when you police once go out to this man's place, he says, remember that you wear a badge and don't turn shit. He's not violating any laws. He says, no law in the state of Texas prohibits the congregation of people who have also raised the state of color. From that decision, which is now, I'm sure, in Texas University, integrated the state of Texas.
You know, I keep thinking that while I'm here, part of what I want to do is get to the libraries and see some of those old newspapers, you know, if you knew the date.
I have some here.
But I would love to see them just to look up the dates on these things so I could get them. I could get them sent over to Tulane, you know, let's swap newspapers back in.
Yeah. But we'd have to research that in there. Yeah. But I don't know if they would have anything like that.
Oh, they say about the public history. You know human history in a case like that.
That's what I'm one with. Yeah. It was such a blow to the other, what I say to the white man. I don't think he likes to let these things know. You know.
But you can't hide something like that.

I know, and that's part of the universities and libraries. Well, the only one that could tell you anything about that is the guys that study law. Yeah. See if this particular case is still on the docket, which I'm sure it would be. Yeah.
I'm sure, sure enough. I'm sure it's gone into the law book.

I was also responsible for integrating most of the bases because I fought the civil rights here. I picketed the Jaskis, walked the pickets, the biggest store in the state of Texas. The handy andy stores, the biggest chain stores in the state of Texas. I walked the picket line. What about all of these things? Now, what I'm referring to on the walking in the pickets lines now is in 1950, 2053. The Keough case was in 52. The bases recently, about six years ago, was at Randolph when I had an investigation from the old school. In 1941, I organized the first Goodwill Society for the benefit of the Negroes at Kennedy.
How did that Goodwill Society work? Actually, I don't know anything about that anymore.

Well, I had the privilege, being a foeman, of going into the higher up of the brackets, meeting the colonels. And then too, I played a little music then, and I would meet these colonels at the officers' club, and they'd invite me to the table to take a drink with them. And in so drinking, or talking with them, I would tell them the situation that was on the base. So they'd say, well okay, we're having fun tonight. See me Monday morning. Monday morning, I would be in his office, and I would explain to him the situation of the Negroes. So Colonel Hicks, he said, why don't you organize? He said, will you give me the privilege? I said, sure. So I organized with the Negroes that I thought that I could depend on. That was the Goodwill Society for the betterment of the Negroes. That was my name. I had given it to him. So when the Colonel, you know how the army works, I mean, they moved the personnel around me, juggled them like a checkerboard. So this Colonel left, and a southern major took over, and he gradually eased me out of what I was doing, and set up a consular for him. And he put what we call, Uncle Tom Negro in charge. So what I was doing, we went down the drain. That was another reason why I went to leave and open the nightclub. So we get back from one thing to the other.
Yeah, you left the Civil Service again.
That was the first time, in 1944.
Oh, and that was in 1944. Oh, I see.
That's why I'm saying I'm going back over a few things that were in my mind. It tears up what I've done. Yeah, it's tearing me up now. Yeah.
You've been in Civil Service a total of twenty?

Well now, if you would compile it from 1941, you would see it goes over the 30. Yeah. With the break in between for the nightclub operation and for the New Orleans Post Office, they've not got four years that are not counted. Yeah. Not four. The Post Office counts because it's Civil Service. So that's why today I have twenty-six years instead of thirty or thirty-one.

So you've had a couple of breaks in there. That's right. I see. You know, I never did get your boy's name Chauncey Highland. Chauncey Highland. How do you spell it? Biggest crook you've ever seen. S-Y-L-E-N-D. H?
Y-L-E-N-D. Yeah. I'd never seen his name written on him. I didn't know how to spell it on him. Right. Well, he confidants Beansy.
I had given up my band in New Orleans. That was the first time. And he confidants Beansy in backing me. Beansy had a son that he wanted to put in business.

So Beansy called me. Beansy and I have been great friends. I told him and I want to sell him out and you probably couldn't help him. I don't want the money, he says I just want him to learn the business. So he financed the deal for about $5,000 and bought this crook of automobile and he got on the road to book the band. He hadn't gotten as far as Austin when he had messed up about five or six days. But I organized my band again. That's when I got Lionel Reason in the band. I don't know if you ever heard of him a piano playing. He's my own. He's my own Louisiana.
He's in Baton Rouge now.

He is. He's a preacher. No kidding. And then Tom Johnson was a saxophone player. And I got through some of my old men back. They wanted to come back in the band. But it didn't last. I had to pick it up again after this guy messed the beans out of his money. And I said, well I'm into it again. I better just go ahead and go to book it again. So I went to book the band again. That's another one of those unfortunate situations that came up. I didn't know I just said. Oh the clock is making them out. I see.
I just wanted to tell you. Did you ever know Nat Tolles? Nat did one of the greatest, which I played with Nat in New Orleans at the theater,

I call him Louisiana. It's that old theater, I think. Right close to the hospital. Used to be a theater there. I can't think of that. Nat used to play in the pit. Yeah. They used jazz bands. Yeah, Flint Goodridge. No, no, no, not. Yeah, that's right. Flint Goodridge. See, when you say Flint Goodridge, I'm going way back, before it was built there, I'm going back to Flint Goodridge up there on the canal. And what is it, the canal. That's where it first went. There was so many hospitals along there. And it was a wooden structure there. Now Flint Goodridge is the one that I'm referring to on Louisiana Avenue. And then Nat and I played together, and then when I was up in Omaha, Nebraska, Nat was a big thing up there. Nat had the first very big traveling van, I mean van, to transport his van that was in the business. And so my bus broke down and Nat said, well, use mine. Let me use this for me. Yeah, we were real close friends. I don't know if you ever knew Nat Jones. He was a lovely person.
I never did know.
Oh, he was a, he could play bass, real good bass player. But he had a heart as big as, big as a house. Had a good band, tremendous band.
But I've heard so much about it, I know. I knew a few people that played with him, like Joe Bentley that's always played. He played the trumpet player.
Yeah.

And of course I've read it, that Sir Charles Thompson plays it. I've read that, I never knew. Who was that? Charles Thompson, the piano player. Well I didn't know the place. You didn't know the men in the band?

No, I didn't know the men in the band. I met them, but to say, get a relationship with them, no I didn't. Did you listen to Nat's band? Oh yeah, sure. In fact we played next to each other. Where was that? New Orleans. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I remember you were playing next to each other.
What was that? New Orleans.
At the Santa Santa Club. That's when you came back, I mean. That was my big band on one of my tours.
Mm-hmm. On one of my tours.
Ah. What's this Clarence Williams, you remember Clarence Williams? Yeah, I remember you talking about. I knew his son.
His son.

He had a band I played against him at the Santa Santa Club. You see they all wanted to play with me down there because whenever I played the Santa Santa Santa Club we turned them away. Now let's don't confuse this.
This is back in the thirties. See, because Nat, uh, uh, Nat left New Orleans.

About the same time that I was in the time that I was in the time that I was in the time that I was in the time that I was in the time that I was in the time that I was in You see they all wanted to play with me down there because whenever I played the Santa Center Club we turned them away. Now these are the days when I had my band, now let's don't confuse this, this is back in the 30's. See because Nat left New Orleans about the same time that I did, he went to Dallas, and he was a big thing in Dallas.
So you knew him there and then New Orleans, yeah you really knew him.
I come up with him. Yeah. Sure, I came up with Nat Toys. Where's he from, what part of the family? Uptown. What we call Uptown from Dallantown.
Yeah, sure. Thanks Amar, what happened at the Dallas State Fair?
In what regard? Well I mean I don't. That was the beginning of my band.
Oh I see.

You see Bernard Goldberg, a Jewish friend of mine that liked me from the first day that he met me. In fact this guy was driving a big black Pierce Hour in those days and he would go into me just like it was my car. So when I quit Charles Band in Dallas and I went back to New Orleans, he came down there and he told me, he said, why don't you get your band? Oh I said Mr. Goldberg, I'm a little too young for that. He said, go ahead and get your band, I'll get a job for you. In fact Bernard Goldberg had already had the job at the State Fair, at the Jewish. So I said, okay. I said, find out how much the men want. So I went around different guys and they all wanted $40, $50 to leave. And the one that I wanted for my drummer was Little Bob. So Little Bob told me that he wanted $40, so he came back two days before we were going to leave and said he needed a party more for his wife. Well that let me know that he didn't want to go anywhere. So finally I saw this fellow, Fats Martin. Little Bob.
Mm-hmm. Bobberman. Yeah. Little.

Look, we never did call him Little Rock on the back. No, no. So I got Fats Martin which was a blessing in disguise. Because this guy turned out to be to me one of the greatest drummers that I'd ever heard. He had a bad tendency though to increase time sometimes. Well sometimes it was bad if we were playing a show similar to the one we played with in Detroit, Michigan. And he had this guy, Pete Peaches of Duke, had great, great dances out of the cotton club. But Pete had gone, Pete Nugent had gone and the singer. The guy could tap without even raising his foot off the floor. But he was very, very particular about his music. And Fats had a tendency to try to follow him with what he was doing and increase or decrease. And this would burn this character up. He could burn which one up? Pete Nugent. Pete Nugent. Because he raised hell with Fats about the time. But that's the only fault that I found the foys of drumming. That's why the band was considered America's greatest swing band. Because we had a tempo of the whole.
And of course that's, we just scratching the surface when we start talking about the foys of your band and everything. How many drummers have you known that didn't increase? How many of them?

I had a number of drummers. A lot of drummers don't increase. Freddie Coleman doesn't increase. He doesn't drop back. Freddie plays identical drums to Fats Martin, which the only difference of his tempo is more sustainable. But sometimes a drummer that's, what we call a show drummer, that's showing out in other words. He has a tendency of increasing or decreasing. Because he's too wrapped up in what he wants to do and then he gets away from the basic part. Well, what you have was, well Joe Jones. Joe Jones never increased a PPS. Same with Billy Payne. Now, Sonny Greer had a tendency of getting away from him. Not a whole lot. You would have to be there to yourself and a musician yourself to feel it. But the ordinary person out there wouldn't be there.
Well, to me, most drummers now, it seems, increase. And, for example, that they don't make drummers like they do.

Well, yeah, that's what you have to take that into consideration. Drummers today don't ruin music. Drummers today, I doubt, seriously, well you're talking about these fly-by-night drummers, but you're not talking about drummers like Harry Belson or drummers like that. Those are seasoned drummers. They don't do things like that. They are Finnish musicians. But you're talking about these rock and rollers. Anything might happen with that.
We were talking about the Dallas State Fair, how your band got started there. What went on at the Dallas State Fair? See, I never was at a...

Well, that's every October. That's a regular, one of the regular celebrations that they have. The world's fast stage fair. And this year, I don't remember what year it was that I was playing with. But it was in October of 1929. And the band that organized in New Orleans out there, Bernard Goldberg, had given me that money. We drove all the way from New Orleans, all the way from New Orleans into Dallas. And that was... Well, maybe I'll say that the Lord's blessed me more ways when one, it was... This was the only engagement that Bernard Goldberg had that was paying me enough money. And he could finance my band. And he could finance the uniforms. But he stayed with the band, booking it. But what happened, a few nights before we closed the State Fair, we didn't know what we were doing. I don't know how this man ever got the phone. I don't know where I was. He was here in San Antonio with Lala Estes. And he called me and asked me, could I come to San Antonio on a job? And it was a job that Troy Floyd was on, the Chicken Plantation. Troy had had a phone out with him and he was giving me his notice. He was going to Oklahoma, which was a blessing for me. So I took the job. And that's how we came on in the San Antonio. We were able to increase the band. We were able to rehearse the band and get it in the shape that he was in. And from that he got into Shatner.
So you added men once the State Fair was over?
I added the first, as soon as I got to Dallas I met Hiram Harding, who had just come into Dallas. And I supplemented him with me, two drumsticks there in the truck. That's how I became the 10 Pounds.
Now when you got to San Antonio, to the Chicken Plantation, did you add any part of him?
Not right then. When we went to Shatnerland we got Philander Tiller. And we had Arthur Durably, Philander Tiller, Amore Cattrack and Hall.
So you got a real close song, didn't you?

That was the first bass song. And then when we went up a little further, when we added Geechee Robinson, another drum roll. We had Nick Turner, another bass record. I had Jimmy Johnson on the string bass. And I had Nick Turner on the Suze for MWM on the drum roll. And then later on I added Harold Holmes, who's now in Canada, who did most of my arranging. And as we traveled over the country, I added here, subtracted, added and subtracted.
And I found the change in the years. Did you ever play any other state fairs? You want to start it by now or is it?

No, no, the state fairs that I can remember. We played places where the fairs were held in such as in Kansas City. We played at the park in that, Farrowland Park. And over here in Waco, Texas, there's a big park there where they used to have them. We played in that one. Yeah, it's quite a number of places where the fairs were held, but never another fair.
Now, what about foreign countries? You say you played in some foreign countries?
Mexico. Mexico.
What was that like?
In what regards? How did I like it or how was the music? Yeah, how did you like it?
What kind of music did you play?
Well, it was alright, but I was at, well not with my band, with Troy.
Oh, you went to Mexico with Troy? I was with Troy.
My band has never played a foreign country.
Oh, I see. You're down out of there. Never, never played in Canada or Mexico.

Well, on the borderline of Canada. Right. And then in Mexico, Reynosa, but you wouldn't call that. You know, that's right there on the border. Yeah, you played. When you said Mexico City, then you're all the way in Mexico.
Yeah, yeah, but not all the way down there.
But at the height of my ambition is to get to some foreign country before it's too late.
Well, of course, you've always, well you've been building a big reputation in foreign countries. But with that, or in Blackstone's right up that one to countries all over the world.

I don't know what the reason for it is, but I never, I'm never able to get someone real interested in getting me to do a concert. So I would like very much to go first of all, to see the country. I love to see new things. And I'm a very sentimentalist. And things like that touch me when I get to these places. And that's been the height of my ambition. I most certainly would want to do a concert. Preferably Europe, because I have some friends in the world. But the first one that would come would be the one that I most certainly would want to do and do it personally. So dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
We were talking about your anniversary.

Yes, it was the 46th anniversary of being married to Hazel, and our daughter was married the same day, so now we have a double anniversary on the 8th of September. Well, it's been 46 beautiful years. Like everything else, it's had its ups and downs. We've had some lean days, we've had some fat days, we've had some in-between days. But all in all, the relationship has been tremendous. We've lived through everything that we could have possibly lived through. Like I said, there's a lot of happy moments to be remembered. And of course, life wouldn't be complete without some sad moments, too. And this life was had on the left. And we're only hoping that our daughter will be able to last as long as we've lasted, and also our son. And it was almost a triple anniversary, because on the 8th of... When we were married on the 8th of September, Kenneth came into the world on the 3rd of September. It's really pretty close.
Well, what did y'all do on this...what did you say, the 42nd anniversary or so? Well...

The 43rd... No, the 44th. It appears to be the 44th. It was the 44th. Well, I didn't think that we would be together much longer, which is only an idea I had in mind, that I wanted to celebrate in a big way and get our wedding blessed at the church, Corpus Christi, where we were married. So I decided that was a good time. So we went down in the audience and we celebrated the 44th year there. And we also combined the concert with this wedding anniversary of our marriage.
And where was that held?
Corpus Christi. Corpus Christi Church.
That's right.

That's where we were originally married in the small Corpus Christi Church, where it was just a small church and has grown to be one of the largest churches in the world, which is predominantly neighborhood.
And Leanna's married since I last saw her. Who?
Lynette.
Well, that's what I say.
She married on our anniversary date. Yeah, I see that. April, 8th of September. Yeah, but we didn't get his name.
His name is... Roy Washington.
Roy Washington.
He's a native of San Antonio? San Antonio native. Nice fellow. He has a degree from St. Louis.
And he's a native of San Antonio. He's a native of San Antonio. Nice fellow. He has a degree from St. Louis. I see. Now, Kenneth has been married how long?
Well, you can figure that from the anniversary. He was born one year after we were married. We celebrated our 46th anniversary.

It has to make him be 45. No, how long has he been married? Oh, how long has he been married? He's been married 21 years. That's a long time. But he also has been a career in the battery. Well, his son has been married 21 years. He's been married 21 years. That's a long time. And... Well, he also has been a career in the battery.
What's his wife's name? She's a maiden name was Garcia.
Janie Garcia. San Antonio. I see. Janie Garcia. Janie Garcia. Janie Garcia. San Antonio.
I see.
Oh, one thing I didn't get.
When the young lady called herself, Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, How do you spell Anise? Anise, Anise, Anise, Anise, how do you spell Anise?
A-N-I-S-E, the original Cotton Club, she was a very beautiful girl, a real small, a petite, as they say. And Anise was a little fella, the most beautiful dance team I've ever seen.
I noticed something in the newspaper yesterday, I guess it was a light, January the 1st, 1934, they told about 1,200 jobless men storming the Court County courthouse. Do you remember that at all?
The 34? I wasn't here, I was traveling.
So you didn't see all that trouble with the men storming the county courthouse, wanting jobs, marching on Washington, those troubles, do you remember any of that?
No, I don't, I wasn't here like I said before, I was traveling east with the band.
Well, any place in the country, did you ever run first jobless men?

No, in New York during the Depression, I've seen them on the soup line. And incidentally, Ben Barth, who had chosen universal attractions, he and I were close friends and we both shared a dinner together.
